newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's move against media owner unleashes protests.
newsitem.headline: Peru's move against media owner unleashes protests.

text.p: The annulment of the citizenship of an Israeli-born television station owner brought a wave of media and public protests against the Peruvian government on Monday.
Several thousand people staged a demonstration outside the offices of Frecuencia Latina in support for its owner Baruch Ivcher, who was stripped of his Peruvian citizenship on Sunday.
The protestors, including journalists, pensioners, students and opposition leaders, waved placards saying "Down with the Dictatorship" and "Long Live Press Freedom!"
The government cancelled Ivcher's citizenship, saying there were irregularities in his application forms.

But journalists employed at Frecuencia Latina said at a news conference that pro-government minority shareholders were seeking to take over the station by getting Ivcher barred. Peruvian law denies foreigners the right to own local media.
The Peruvian media, including normally pro-government ones, unanimously condemned the revocation of Ivcher's citizenship.

"Independent journalism, institutions unbowed by the government's steam roller, and citizens at large, must close ranks in these circumstances and energetically protest to stop the escalating anti-democratic process," Peru's respected independent newspaper El Comercio said in an editorial.
Ivcher, who is in Miami due to alleged political persecution and death-threats, called the move "barbarous."
"They are committing horrible abuses, first against my rights, then against my property," Ivcher said in a radio interview from Miami.
Analysts said the measure was no coincidence following a string of stories by Frecuencia Latina alleging corruption and rights abuses in President Alberto Fujimori's security forces.
Attorney General Miguel Aljovin promised on Monday to investigate Frecuencia Latina's latest allegation that Peru's secret services had carried out systematic phone-tapping.

The government said there were omissions in Ivcher's application forms and no proof that he gave up his Israeli nationality. The citizenship documents were, however, signed and approved in 1984 by former President Fernando Belaunde, who denied on Monday that there had been any irregularities.
